extraction.name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
extraction.description: This paper presents a systematic study on object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs), where LVLMs tend to generate objects inconsistent with the target images in descriptions. The study evaluates several representative LVLMs and finds that they suffer from severe object hallucination issues. The paper introduces a polling-based query method called POPE to better evaluate object hallucination in LVLMs, demonstrating that POPE can evaluate hallucination in a more stable and flexible way compared to traditional methods like CHAIR.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.citeAs: Li, Y., Du, Y., Zhou, K., Wang, J., Zhao, W. X., & Wen, J. R. (2023). Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2305.10355.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset used for evaluation is MSCOCO (Common Objects in Context), a large-scale image recognition, segmentation, and captioning dataset. The study evaluates LVLMs on 2,000 randomly sampled images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions from MSCOCO's validation set. The evaluation focuses on 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MSCOCO dataset, which includes images with annotations about contained objects and human-labeled captions.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The study uses the CHAIR metric to evaluate object hallucination, which requires parsing generated captions to extract predicted objects using human-crafted complex rules. The paper also introduces POPE, a polling-based method that converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with simple Yes-or-No questions about probing objects.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include ground-truth objects in images and human-labeled captions. The study also uses automatic segmentation tools like SEEM to annotate images for unannotated datasets. The POPE method constructs triples consisting of an image, multiple questions, and their answers (Yes or No) to evaluate hallucination.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic segmentation, and human annotators for ground-truth object annotations and captions.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The study analyzes the correlation between the appearance frequency of objects in the visual instruction dataset and their hallucination times in LVLMs. It also examines the impact of different sampling strategies (Random, Popular, Adversarial) on hallucination evaluation.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once), CHAIR metric for evaluation, and POPE for hallucination evaluation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper discusses the social implications of object hallucination in LVLMs, noting that hallucination can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications, such as safety issues in autonomous driving systems. The study aims to mitigate these issues by evaluating and addressing object hallucination in LVLMs.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The study finds that LVLMs are prone to hallucinate objects that frequently appear or co-occur in the visual instruction dataset. This bias is attributed to the unbalanced object distribution in the visual instruction data, where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The paper acknowledges several limitations, including: (1) The study only focuses on object hallucination and does not measure the overall performance of LVLMs. (2) The evaluation is conducted on a subset of the validation set due to computational resource limitations. (3) POPE may inaccurately evaluate LVLMs if they fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers. (4) The use of automatic segmentation tools like SEEM may lead to inconsistencies with human annotations. (5) The study only evaluates a small number of LVLMs and does not include recently released or closed-source models.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset and evaluation methods are used for Training, Testing, and Validation of LVLMs to assess their object hallucination issues. The POPE method is designed to provide a stable, fair, and flexible evaluation approach for object hallucination in LVLMs.
